title: IBM goes big to keep quantum computers cold
description:
IBM connected two large, ultracold cryogenic modules, clearing an engineering hurdle on the way to a much larger quantum computer.
IBM said its modular architecture could eventually link hundreds of quantum chips and support its plan to build IBM Quantum Starling, the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, targeted for 2029.
IBM said L-couplers allow separate quantum chips to share information, communicate and operate as parts of a larger quantum computer.
IBM said the design incorporated three essential components from the environment used in IBM Quantum System Two while allowing engineers to test, improve and rapidly iterate on each component independently.
IBM said it plans to install IBM Quantum Nighthawk processors in the cryogenic modules later this year to expand operational performance testing.
text:
IBM connected two large, ultracold cryogenic modules, clearing an engineering hurdle on the way to a much larger quantum computer.

The new system tackles a practical problem facing efforts to scale quantum computing: how to keep growing numbers of quantum processors cold enough to operate while giving engineers enough space to connect them. IBM said its modular architecture could eventually link hundreds of quantum chips and support its plan to build IBM Quantum Starling, the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, targeted for 2029.

Fault tolerance aims to let a quantum computer continue operating reliably despite errors by detecting and correcting them. IBM said Starling would combine advances in error correction, processor design, decoding and systems engineering.

“The successful connection and operation of these cryogenic modules signals a leap forward in that direction,” Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow, said in IBM’s announcement.

Superconducting quantum processors operate at ultracold temperatures. IBM said its first two connected cryogenic modules jointly reached 4 Kelvin, roughly the temperature of liquid helium, in less than five days, then cooled to below 15 millikelvin.

IBM said the larger enclosure also created more room for wiring. Each module’s vacuum enclosure offered up to 12 times more wiring space than the enclosures in its most widely used IBM quantum systems, according to the company. The additional space enabled more chip-to-chip connections within individual modules and between separate modules.

The company designed the box-shaped modules to connect in a tight row. This layout created room to link separate quantum processors directly through IBM’s L-coupler technology. IBM said L-couplers allow separate quantum chips to share information, communicate and operate as parts of a larger quantum computer.

This modular architecture also gives IBM a way to work on parts of the cryogenic system separately. IBM said the design incorporated three essential components from the environment used in IBM Quantum System Two while allowing engineers to test, improve and rapidly iterate on each component independently.

According to IBM, the approach could help the company speed up development of the cryogenic infrastructure needed for larger quantum systems.

The next stage will put quantum processors inside the new cooling system. IBM said it plans to install IBM Quantum Nighthawk processors in the cryogenic modules later this year to expand operational performance testing.

In the announcement, IBM’s roadmap called for L-couplers to connect multiple processors in a larger quantum computer with at least 1,000 programmable qubits by 2027. Qubits are the basic units of information in a quantum computer, and IBM defines programmable qubits as those that can be directly used to perform computations. By the time IBM delivers Starling in 2029, the company said each cryogenic module could house thousands of programmable qubits.

Cooling represents one part of a broader quantum computing effort. IBM introduced its plans for Starling last year alongside a new error-correction code that the company said dramatically reduced the physical resources required for fault tolerance. Since then, IBM said it has demonstrated core hardware components and made progress on more efficient error-correction decoding.

The work “will accelerate our progress alongside continued innovation in quantum hardware, software, and algorithms,” Gambetta said.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO – Hyundai Motor is considering plans to further expand its U.S. production at a new multibillion-dollar vehicle assembly plant in Georgia, CEO José Muñoz told CNBC on Thursday.

Muñoz said the South Korean automaker could increase the planned production capacity of its Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America from 500,000 units to between 700,000 and 800,000 units by 2028.

"For us, the USA is the most important market in the world besides Korea, which is our headquarters," Muñoz said Thursday during an exclusive interview after the reveal of the company's flagship Genesis GV90 SUV.

The potential capacity increase would be part of Hyundai's plan to invest $26 billion in the U.S. through 2028, he said. The company aims to launch dozens of new products and has a goal to produce at least 80% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. domestically by the end of this decade, up from roughly 40% in 2024.

"For that purpose, we need to add more more capacity," he said Thursday. "We want to have all this up and running by 2028. That is our intention."

Following publication, Hyundai said the plans are under consideration but not yet confirmed.

The plans would likely make the plant the largest vehicle assembly operation by capacity in the U.S., overtaking other facilities from companies such as Tesla and Toyota Motor .

Hyundai is also evaluating additional investment for capacity outside of the Georgia Metaplant for body-on-frame vehicles such as trucks and SUVs, but Muñoz declined to disclose further details.

"We are always, always assessing the opportunities that we have in the market," he said.

Muñoz said President Donald Trump's tariffs, including 15% on imports from South Korea, have played a role in the company accelerating its U.S. production plans.

"Tariffs are helping accelerate our localization plan. That's very, very simple," he said. "The good thing is that we had already started before tariffs were announced. So in a way it's helping us to accelerate."

Hyundai initially announced the plant in 2022 but it has continued to increase its plans for the $7.6 billion facility that's designated to produce hybrid and all-electric vehicles for Hyundai, Genesis and its corporate sibling Kia.

The Metaplant currently produces the all-electric Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 as well as the Kia Sportage hybrid.

Muñoz, who became the first non-Korean CEO of the automaker when he took the role last year, said the company's plans include producing a variety of different vehicles at the plant and employing thousands. The current plan for 500,000 units included more than 8,500 employees on the Georgia megasite and an additional 6,900 people at offsite suppliers.

Hyundai has experienced massive U.S. sales growth this decade, even before the Metaplant came online. Sales for the brand and the parent company, which includes Kia and Genesis, are up nearly 50%, according to company reports and Mobility Global.

Hyundai has increased its market share in the U.S. from 8.4% in 2020 to 11.2% last year, according to Mobility Global, formerly known as S&P Global Mobility.

title: Nvidia seeks China AI comeback with new chip designed for local market: Report
description:
Nvidia has started shipping small volumes of a new AI chip designed for Chinese customers, with shipments expected to increase by the end of the year, according to a report by The Information on Thursday.
The chip is designed to work alongside primary graphics processors to accelerate AI model response times.
Several Chinese companies have already placed orders for the new device, setting up a direct challenge to domestic AI hardware such as Huawei Technologies’ upcoming Ascend 950DT.
Shortage of computing capacity in China Nvidia’s move to supply China comes as the country’s AI sector faces a growing shortage of computing capacity.

text:
Nvidia has started shipping small volumes of a new AI chip designed for Chinese customers, with shipments expected to increase by the end of the year, according to a report by The Information on Thursday. The new offering is reportedly a modified version of Nvidia’s language processing unit (LPU), developed using licensed technology from Groq. The chip is designed to work alongside primary graphics processors to accelerate AI model response times.

Since Nvidia’s Vera Rubin architecture cannot be exported to China under current US restrictions, engineers have modified the LPU’s software so that the hardware can operate alongside other processors that are permitted in the country.

Several Chinese companies have already placed orders for the new device, setting up a direct challenge to domestic AI hardware such as Huawei Technologies’ upcoming Ascend 950DT. However, shipments still require regulatory approval from Beijing, which has previously restricted the use of foreign silicon as part of efforts to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturers.

Shortage of computing capacity in China

Nvidia’s move to supply China comes as the country’s AI sector faces a growing shortage of computing capacity. Chinese AI companies are dealing with severe computing bottlenecks, with the strain already leading Moonshot AI to freeze new sign-ups and DeepSeek to raise developer fees. With China’s largest technology companies working to expand domestic chip production through 2027, the current shortage could give Nvidia a crucial window to re-engage Chinese customers before they permanently transition to locally developed architectures.

The initiative highlights Nvidia’s efforts to preserve its presence in the Chinese market despite Washington’s export controls and earlier comments from CEO Jensen Huang suggesting that the company had largely conceded the region to Huawei. Nvidia is also scaling shipments of its cleared H200 processors, with packaging partner Amkor Technology reportedly finishing more than one million units in the second quarter. The company is also developing lower-power gaming chips specifically for the Chinese market.

text: That was not a good report from Walmart . While the nation's largest brick-and-mortar retailer reported fiscal second-quarter earnings and revenue that beat analyst expectations, same-store sales only grew by 2.6% compared to last year — well below a FactSet consensus forecast of 3.5%. Mizuho analyst David Bellinger called that comparable store sales whiff "one of the biggest misses in years." Couple that with disappointing earnings guidance for the fiscal third quarter and the full year, and you have what Bellinger referred to as the "worst case scenario" for Walmart. Shares were down 7% in early trading, on pace for their worst day since May 21. The report also raises a major question for the wider stock market: Is consumer spending, one of the key pillars of the economy, starting to slow down? "The slowdown in the funnel challenges the market's bull case," wrote Morgan Stanley analyst Simeon Gutman. WMT 5D mountain WMT 5-day chart Walmart CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that consumers are stretched thin, particularly as energy prices continue to climb. U.S. crude futures are up 53% this year thanks to the U.S.-Iran war. Rainey also said that while Walmart is eligible to receive about $2.9 billion in tariff refunds, Walmart expects to take a roughly $2 billion hit from "incremental cost headwinds related to higher fuel prices this year." "Consumers are still spending, and real wage growth is keeping pace, and so they've been very resilient in this environment," Rainey said . "But all that said, we would love to be able to bring prices down more and see less pressure on their wallets." Combine uncertainty over consumer spending with another increase in oil prices — U.S. crude futures rose more than 2% Thursday to around $88 per barrel — and Treasury yields again moving higher, and you get a downbeat start to the trading day. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost more than 400 points, while S & P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures slid 0.4% and 0.6%, respectively. But ,to be sure, other analysts who cover Walmart remain bullish on the stock. Oliver Chen of TD Cowen, who rates the Bentonville, Arkansas-based behemoth a buy, is "encouraged by WMT's ability to gain share and grow profits faster than sales." KeyBanc analyst Bradley Thomas called Walmart's headwinds "transitory" and reiterated an overweight investment rating. But if those constructive outlooks don't pan out, it could mean trouble not just for Walmart — but for the entire stock market.

text:
Sales at the US retail giant Walmart grew at their slowest pace for more than six years in the most recent quarter, suggesting American shoppers are under strain.

Walmart, which due to its size is well-placed to gauge consumers' mood, blamed the rising price of fuel.

Sales at comparable sites across the chain were up by 2.6%, excluding fuel, between May and July the company said.

Walmart said it would use up to $3bn of expected tariff refunds to lower prices in a bid to keep customers spending.

The rebate stems from duties the retailer paid after President Trump imposed a wave of tariffs on imported goods last year. Retailers are receiving refunds from central government after those tariffs were ruled unlawful.

Walmart, the US's largest retailer, said the nearly $3bn in tariff rebate it anticipated would help it continue a programme of price cuts or "rollbacks" that it expanded earlier this year.

Walmart has leaned heavily on price cuts to retain customers, launching 11,000 of its so-called "rollbacks" across categories.

Chief financial officer John David Rainey said those lower prices were already lifting transactions and unit sales, especially in food and other staples like toys.

But he acknowledged that the retail environment remained uneven, with lower-income households – a core part of Walmart's base – feeling squeezed.

Rainey said rising petrol prices were leaving shoppers with less spare cash, saying the shift in behaviour became clear once fuel went above $4 a gallon.

Price moves in June made the impact obvious, he added, with lower-income customers pulling back and focusing spending on essentials.

Beyond the consumer pullback, Walmart's results highlighted several additional risks that could shape the firm's prospects in the months ahead.

Much of the quarter's profit lift came from tariff refunds that had already come in, a one-off benefit that analysts say won't recur to the same extent.

The price rollbacks could put pressure on margins, while Walmart is also spending money on automation, new warehouses, and tech upgrades.

On the earnings call, analysts pressed management on whether lower prices were already driving a lift in sales and whether some rollbacks could be locked in for 2027.

Walmart said the benefits were showing up most clearly in food and other staples, and that certain cuts might remain if they continued to resonate with shoppers.

"Our hope and intention always is that rollbacks can become permanent ... wherever possible," Rainey said.

Alibaba Cloud held 38.1 percent of China’s AI cloud market in 2025, according to Omdia data cited by Alibaba.
Alibaba E-commerce Revenue Rises 4% to RMB205.862 Billion Alibaba E-commerce Group generated RMB205.862 billion in quarterly revenue, up 4 percent from RMB198.812 billion.
Alibaba AI Capex Jumps 75% to US$9.975 Billion Alibaba accelerated infrastructure spending to support rising AI demand.
While overall revenue grew 9 percent and AI Cloud revenue expanded 45 percent, the company increased capital expenditure by 75 percent and absorbed significantly higher AI investment costs.
text:
Alibaba has reported RMB268.953 billion in revenue for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up 9 percent from RMB247.652 billion a year earlier, as rapid growth in AI cloud and quick commerce helped offset weakness in its core China e-commerce business.

Profitability came under pressure as Alibaba accelerated investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and applications. Income from operations fell 57 percent to RMB15.161 billion from RMB34.988 billion, while net income plunged 75 percent to RMB10.444 billion from RMB42.382 billion.

Adjusted EBITA declined 30 percent to RMB27.329 billion, while non-GAAP net income decreased 38 percent to RMB20.715 billion.

Alibaba AI Cloud Revenue Grows 45%

AI Cloud and Compute Services emerged as Alibaba’s strongest growth engine, with revenue rising 45 percent to RMB48.437 billion (US$7.139 billion) from RMB33.418 billion. Revenue from external customers also expanded 45 percent, driven by increasing adoption of AI-related products.

Adjusted EBITA for AI Cloud and Compute Services surged 133 percent to RMB5.628 billion (US$830 million) from RMB2.419 billion, reflecting revenue growth and improving operating efficiency despite continued investment in customer acquisition and technology.

AI-related product revenue reached RMB12.376 billion (US$1.824 billion), accounting for about 35 percent of external cloud revenue. AI revenue recorded its 12th consecutive quarter of triple-digit year-over-year growth, while its annualized revenue run rate reached approximately RMB49.5 billion (US$7.3 billion).

Alibaba Cloud held 38.1 percent of China’s AI cloud market in 2025, according to Omdia data cited by Alibaba.

Alibaba is also strengthening its AI infrastructure through T-Head Semiconductor’s proprietary portfolio spanning GPUs, CPUs, storage and networking chips. Its Zhenwu chips, including the latest Zhenwu M890 AI processor, have been commercially adopted through Alibaba Cloud by more than 650 external customers across over 20 industries, including autonomous driving, internet and financial services.

Alibaba E-commerce Revenue Rises 4% to RMB205.862 Billion

Alibaba E-commerce Group generated RMB205.862 billion in quarterly revenue, up 4 percent from RMB198.812 billion. Adjusted EBITA slipped 1 percent to RMB39.749 billion (US$5.858 billion) from RMB39.988 billion.

China E-commerce revenue declined 8 percent to RMB110.900 billion (US$16.345 billion) from RMB120.874 billion. Customer management revenue decreased 7 percent, although it would have increased 1 percent on a like-for-like basis excluding the contra-revenue impact.

Direct sales, logistics and other China E-commerce revenue fell 10 percent to RMB28.353 billion (US$4.179 billion) from RMB31.675 billion.

China Quick Commerce delivered much stronger growth, with revenue surging 45 percent to RMB53.295 billion (US$7.855 billion) from RMB36.725 billion, supported by Freshippo and Taobao Instant Commerce.

International E-commerce revenue decreased 1 percent to RMB27.761 billion (US$4.091 billion) from RMB28.177 billion, while Global Wholesale revenue increased 7 percent to RMB13.906 billion (US$2.049 billion).

Alibaba E-commerce Group’s revenue mix comprised approximately 54 percent China E-commerce, 26 percent China Quick Commerce, 13 percent International E-commerce and 7 percent Global Wholesale.

Qwen AI Shopping Reaches 250 Million Users

AI Labs and Applications revenue increased 16 percent to RMB3.338 billion (US$492 million) from RMB2.882 billion.

Heavy investment weighed on profitability, with the segment’s adjusted EBITA loss widening to RMB13.861 billion (US$2.043 billion) from a loss of RMB3.224 billion a year earlier. Alibaba attributed the increase primarily to investments in AI capabilities and higher inference costs associated with the Qwen app.

Alibaba launched Qwen3.8-Max within three months of the previous version and opened the model weights with 2.4 trillion parameters.

The Qwen app is also becoming more closely integrated with Alibaba’s commerce ecosystem. 250 million users have had their first AI-driven shopping experience through Qwen’s agentic features.

Alibaba AI Capex Jumps 75% to US$9.975 Billion

Alibaba accelerated infrastructure spending to support rising AI demand. Quarterly capital expenditure surged 75 percent to RMB67.678 billion (US$9.975 billion) from RMB38.676 billion a year earlier.

The increase reflected continued AI infrastructure investment, higher CPU compute capacity to support anticipated adoption of AI agents, procurement-cycle changes and higher chip-component prices.

The investment surge contributed to free cash flow deteriorating to negative RMB44.670 billion, compared with negative RMB18.815 billion a year earlier.

Alibaba also reduced sales and marketing expenses excluding share-based compensation from RMB52.720 billion to RMB47.288 billion, lowering the ratio from 21.3 percent to 17.6 percent of revenue. General and administrative expenses excluding share-based compensation increased from RMB6.240 billion to RMB11.642 billion, rising from 2.5 percent to 4.3 percent of revenue.

Alibaba’s June 2026 results underline its increasingly aggressive AI strategy. While overall revenue grew 9 percent and AI Cloud revenue expanded 45 percent, the company increased capital expenditure by 75 percent and absorbed significantly higher AI investment costs. The contrast was reflected in net income falling 75 percent, even as AI Cloud adjusted EBITA jumped 133 percent and China Quick Commerce revenue grew 45 percent.

title: Nvidia's Bold AI Investing Strategy Could Soon Backfire – Here's Why - MarketWise
description:
Let’s look at Nvidia’s investments, the company’s strategy, and what the Intel and SpaceX deals mean for the AI industry.
What’s Behind Nvidia’s AI Investment Strategy?
All of top 10 most-funded AI startups on the Forbes AI 50 list of privately held AI companies received investments from Nvidia.
Because if AI companies can’t secure enough GPU power, AI growth slows.
By investing in these AI startups, Nvidia not only opens the door for those companies to buy Nvidia products, but it also expands Nvidia’s AI imprint across the globe.
text:
Listen to the audio version of this article (generated by AI).

When you’re the world’s most valuable company – with a market capitalization of roughly $5.27 trillion – like Nvidia (NVDA), you don’t necessarily need to find new ways to build onto that mind-blowing figure. After all, Nvidia would continue to rake in money if it kept making and selling its innovative chips and artificial-intelligence (“AI”) platforms.

But Nvidia didn’t become the world’s most valuable company through luck or by resting on its laurels. Nvidia innovates… and it invests. And those investments are laying the groundwork for the next phase of Nvidia’s AI strategy.

Between 2021 and 2025, Nvidia participated in 283 funding rounds involving 241 different companies. Many of those companies (nearly 85%) were AI startups, including existing and potential future competitors.

Nvidia then doubled down in late 2025 when it finalized a $5 billion equity investment in American chipmaker Intel (INTC). And just last week, Nvidia disclosed a nearly $21 billion stake in SpaceX (SPCX) in the form of roughly 122.8 million shares – enough stock to make Nvidia the sixth-largest investor in Elon Musk’s sprawling venture.

Nvidia’s investment strategy appears to be paying off so far. But key risks remain. Let’s look at Nvidia’s investments, the company’s strategy, and what the Intel and SpaceX deals mean for the AI industry.

What’s Behind Nvidia’s AI Investment Strategy?

Short answer: Money. As in, Nvidia literally has so much money, it doesn’t know what to do with it all. So, it invests to make more money.

It’s undeniable that there’s plenty of strategy behind Nvidia’s investments. In fact, investing is part of Nvidia’s business strategy.

The company literally wrote a blog post about it on Nvidia’s website. According to Nvidia, the company takes a three-pronged approach toward investing.

First, through Nvidia’s corporate investments, overseen by [Vishal] Bhagwati. Second, through NVentures, our venture capital arm, led by [Sid] Siddeek. And finally, through Nvidia Inception, our vehicle for supporting startups and connecting them to venture capital.

So, Nvidia makes direct investments, invests in startups, and helps train those startups on the Nvidia platform and ecosystem.

And the company’s investments are vast:

In 2023, Nvidia was the fourth-largest corporate venture investor, behind only Microsoft (MSFT), SoftBank (SFTBY), and Alphabet (GOOGL).

Of the 241 companies Nvidia invested in between 2021 and 2025, six received at least three investments from Nvidia, including AI startups Cohere (four times), Perplexity AI (four times), and Mistral AI (three times).

All of top 10 most-funded AI startups on the Forbes AI 50 list of privately held AI companies received investments from Nvidia. Among those were competitors such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

Here you can see just how much Nvidia’s investments in AI startups have increased over the past five years.

Nvidia’s roster of investments includes:

Roughly $30 billion in OpenAI, which includes agreements for OpenAI to buy Nvidia systems

$2 billion each to neocloud leaders CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS), data-center connectivity standout Marvell Technology (MRVL), chip-design software company Synopsys (SNPS), and global photonics leaders Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE)

Up to $2.1 billion in data-center operator Iren (IREN)

Up to $3.2 billion in Corning (GLW) for specialized glass and optical connectivity

These deals often represent a win-win for both Nvidia and whichever company receives its money and/or backing. For the startups, the reason why is rather obvious. They receive a boatload of capital (that they might not otherwise have access to) from the world’s most valuable company – not to mention the huge, invaluable reputational boost that comes with being an Nvidia partner.

Finding the win for Nvidia, however, requires some deeper digging. But it lies in graphics processing unit (“GPU”) access – or the lack thereof for most startup companies. GPU computing power is expensive, so most startups don’t have the financial means to acquire it.

That poses a problem for Nvidia. Because if AI companies can’t secure enough GPU power, AI growth slows. For Nvidia, that’s bad for business.

So Nvidia gives those companies the money they need to access the computing power necessary to grow. If that sounds self-serving, well, it is. Nvidia is essentially financing smaller AI companies so they can purchase the hardware and platforms their businesses need… That hardware and those platforms happen to be built and sold by Nvidia.

That’s called a massive strategic advantage. And it’s pretty brilliant.

By investing in these AI startups, Nvidia not only opens the door for those companies to buy Nvidia products, but it also expands Nvidia’s AI imprint across the globe.

Of course, this also raises questions about the authenticity of the larger AI market since these investments can be considered circular financing.

IDC (International Data Corporation), a Boston-based global market-intelligence firm, summed up circular AI financing perfectly:

Circular financing in AI describes investment structures where the same capital flows simultaneously as vendor payment and equity stake. A company funds its own customer’s revenue while also supplying that customer’s core infrastructure. The result is reported revenue growth that is real but not cleanly separable from investment activity.

While it’s not explicitly illegal, circular AI financing raises ethical concerns. Especially when you consider that these investments have helped companies like Nvidia buy access to startups’ services and technologies without acquiring the company and going through a strict acquisition or merger review process.

You can decide on the ethics. But the strategy has clearly paid off so far for Nvidia and many of the startups it has invested in.

But Nvidia’s investment strategy isn’t limited to small AI companies.

Nvidia’s Massive Investments in Intel and SpaceX, Plus Its Wall Street Partnership

Intel

Nvidia grabbed some headlines last December when it finalized a purchase of roughly 214.7 million shares of Intel stock at $23.28 per share. That came to about $5 billion in shares, and it bought Nvidia a 4% slice of Intel.

Since then, Intel’s stock has exploded. At $92.80 per share (as of August 19), that investment is now worth roughly $19.9 billion. At its peak, when Intel stock reached roughly $140 near the end of June, that investment was valued at a little more than $30 billion.

The money, as if Nvidia needs more, is great. But it’s what Nvidia’s investment in Intel bought that matters just as much, if not more.

As part of this investment, Intel builds custom x86 central processing units (“CPUs”) with Nvidia NVLink integration for AI infrastructure within data centers. Intel also develops system-on-chips (“SoCs”) that combine its CPU cores with Nvidia RTX GPU chiplets for personal computing.

Put simply, Nvidia’s investment builds a bridge between its own architecture and Intel’s. And that matters given Intel has been a top competitor to Nvidia for years.

SpaceX

Just last week, Nvidia disclosed a stake of nearly $21 billion – roughly 122.8 million shares at $170.86 per share – in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led space and AI company. The investment was originally a $10 billion stake in xAI that converted to SpaceX shares after Musk’s SpaceX acquired, yes, Musk’s xAI.

(With SpaceX stock down to roughly $140 as of August 19, Nvidia’s stake is now valued around $17.2 billion.)

Nvidia is now the sixth-largest investor in SpaceX, and SpaceX is now Nvidia’s second-largest equity holding… behind only Intel.

Again, this represents a big win for both parties. Nvidia holds a significant stake in a highly ambitious (though quite volatile) company, and SpaceX builds its AI data centers only with Nvidia chips. There’s that circular pattern again – Nvidia invests in SpaceX, SpaceX buys Nvidia’s products, the resulting innovation elevates SpaceX’s stock price, and Nvidia’s stake grows more valuable.

Wall Street Asset-Management Firms

With investments in Intel and SpaceX seemingly not enough for Nvidia, the chip bellwether decided earlier this month to partner with six of Wall Street’s biggest asset managers – Blackstone (BX), Apollo Global Management (APO), BlackRock (BLK), Brookfield Asset Management (BAM), Goldman Sachs (GS), and KKR (KKR).

The goal? Raise $500 billion in funds to help enterprises, hyperscalers, and frontier AI labs build data centers and buy essential hardware. Why? So Nvidia’s smaller customers – both current and potential – can afford to buy from the company without financing through loans that carry high interest rates.

Through this Wall Street alliance, the asset-management firms involved would underwrite the AI hardware – such as data centers, GPUs, and networking – to secure the multibillion-dollar loans that would contribute to the overall $500 billion goal. Essentially, Nvidia’s hardware that is being leased or purchased serves as an investable asset, like real estate.

A key stipulation in this partnership is that Nvidia will backstop up to 25% of certain projects to help lower interest rates, keep demand steady, and reassure lenders if things go sideways.

Key Risks These Investments Pose for Nvidia

To be clear, investing in AI comes with a high level of risk, whether it’s a simple $1,000 investment in AI-related stock or Nvidia purchasing $5 billion worth of shares from Intel. The advantage for individual investors: They aren’t nearly as reliant on AI continuing to boom as Nvidia is.

AI and data centers now represent more than 90% of Nvidia’s revenue. If the AI bubble bursts, Nvidia would be heavily exposed.

Nvidia’s own business would undoubtedly take a massive hit. But its investments would be in severe jeopardy as well, given how many AI companies it has stakes in. Nvidia could lose hundreds of billions of dollars in an instant.

Given the circular nature of those investments, any downturn that hits AI startups and other businesses Nvidia has invested in would be felt twice as hard by Nvidia and its investors.

What This Means for Nvidia’s Stock

If you’re factoring Nvidia’s own investments into determining whether you want to invest in Nvidia, you’re not likely to get very far with your decision.

It’s truly a mixed bag that presents several benefits such as locking AI startups into Nvidia’s very sticky ecosystem and using AI computing power as a financeable asset to raise hundreds of billions of dollars from Wall Street for smaller AI companies to borrow.

But Nvidia’s investments also expose the company’s own capital to risk through backstopping projects and offering credit support. And Nvidia’s circular dealings could backfire spectacularly should the AI sector experience a major pullback.

All that said, Nvidia has been an excellent stock to own. While its 15% year-to-date gains are more modest than, say, Intel’s at 136% or Micron Technology’s (MU) at 197%, Nvidia’s strong earnings push the stock to a “very bullish” rating from legendary Wall Street veteran Marc Chaikin’s Chaikin Power Gauge, a 20-factor stock-rating system that scans more than 5,000 stocks and 2,300 exchange-traded funds.

While AI stocks are risky and volatile, I don’t see the AI bubble – if one even exists – bursting anytime soon. And Nvidia has earned its status as the global king of AI. Its investments only reinforce that status.

Regards,

David Engle

text:
For the better part of the last four years, the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has ruled the roost on Wall Street. Empowering software and systems with the tools to make split-second, autonomous decisions is an estimated $15.7 trillion addressable opportunity by 2030, according to PwC.

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has led the way. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) are the brains of AI-accelerated data centers, and no company is particularly close to matching the compute capabilities of its hardware.

But what you may not realize is that Wall Street's largest publicly traded company is also an investor.

Just like institutional investors, companies with at least $100 million in assets under management are required to file Form 13F with regulators no later than 45 calendar days after the end of a quarter. Nvidia's latest 13F, detailing second-quarter investment activity for its $63.4 billion portfolio, revealed a new No. 2 holding: Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) (NASDAQ: SPCX).

SpaceX is now Nvidia's second-largest public investment

According to a person familiar with the matter, per CNBC, Nvidia invested roughly $10 billion in xAI in January 2026, as part of a $20 billion funding round for the AI start-up. SpaceX acquired xAI shortly thereafter.

When SpaceX went public on June 12 in Wall Street's largest-ever initial public offering (IPO), it meant that Nvidia would now need to report its stake in the company on its quarterly 13F. This position, 122,764,805 shares of SpaceX, was worth nearly $21 billion at the end of June. Only Nvidia's stake in chipmaker Intel is worth more.

Although the initial buzz from SpaceX's IPO was unlike anything we'd ever seen, reality is starting to bite for Nvidia's new No. 2 holding.

Despite a 92% increase in second-quarter sales, SpaceX reported a hefty loss and eye-popping capital expenditures (capex) for its data center segment. Through the first six months of 2026, AI capex has vaulted from $3.32 billion last year to $23.55 billion this year. Musk's company is burning cash at an alarming rate and is expected to lean on potentially dilutive financing rounds to make up for it.

Furthermore, SpaceX has one of Wall Street's more unique lockup periods, and it's not exactly shareholder-friendly. Whereas most newly public companies prevent insiders (high-ranking executives, board members, and early investors) from selling their stock for 180 calendar days after the IPO, SpaceX's unlock schedule is accelerated and staggered. Several event- and time-based unlocks occur that can dramatically increase the float and weigh on SpaceX's shares.

The argument can also be made that SpaceX has an Elon Musk problem. Aside from splitting his duties between two trillion-dollar companies -- he's also the CEO of electric-vehicle maker Tesla -- Musk doesn't have the best track record of delivering on innovations. Several of his claims at Tesla, such as Level 5 full self-driving being available "next year" or 1 million robotaxis being on public roads by the end of 2020, haven't come to fruition.

While Nvidia has thus far cleaned up with its initial xAI investment, the outlook for SpaceX stock is murky at best.

text:
AI-chip company Nvidia has leaned heavily into corporate venture tools in building the company, investing some $100bn in the past few years into AI startups. It has already realised tens of billions of dollars in paper returns from the sale of portfolio companies xAI and Cursor to SpaceX, as the FT reports.

Nvidia was itself the recipient of corporate venture backing from SEGA during its nascent years, and understands the power of the model. Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO, joked about SoftBank’s failure to hold Nvidia stock long term — SoftBank acquired a 4.9% stake in Nvidia in 2017, valued at about $4bn, but sold it off by 2019. Masa Son’s conglomerate would have earned nearly $1trn if it had held on to its position in what is now a business worth $5.5tn.

But the real gains from CVC investment for Nvidia are not the returns from exits — it is the way these investments are used to create aligned business relationships. SpaceX, for example, has an exclusive relationship with Nvidia to use its AI tech to build out its planned near-10GW data centre by the end of next year.

SpaceX will be a large user of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin processors, with some $150bn to $300bn in real cash flowing into Nvidia’s books. That is about a 20th of Nvidia’s current market value of more than $3bn — a high price-to-sales multiple for a hardware company but reflecting Nvidia’s strong market position and the “stickiness” of the services ecosystem that users of its chip enter into. It is also interesting to note that the market takes a much more positive view of buying equity stakes in a customer than it does of traditional vendor finance deals.

Now, that’s strategic if you are a CEO of any business.

Italy's UniCredit has moved one step closer to a majority stake in Commerzbank. Commerzbank has canceled its most recently repurchased shares, according to a voting-rights notification released on Thursday. As a result, without any action of its own, the Italians now have access to as much as 49.65% of Commerzbank, up from 47.59% previously. However, 3.36% of that total still consists of call options that UniCredit can convert into Commerzbank shares at any time.

This does not change the balance of power at the annual general meeting, because treasury shares do not carry voting rights. In addition, UniCredit would already have controlled a majority there, because in practice almost never are all shareholders represented.

The Frankfurt-based lender had so far held 4.14% of its share capital in treasury shares, which it had repurchased from shareholders in recent years to distribute excess capital. It had announced it would cancel them, but long delayed doing so amid the dispute over a UniCredit takeover.

text:
Levi Strauss & Co is betting on India to play a pivotal role in its ambition to become a $10 billion company. The denim major sees headroom for growth not just in jeans but across women’s wear, tops, and premium products.

“India has always been referred to as one of the pivotal countries that will contribute to this ambition in a big way,” Hiren Gor, Managing Director, South Asia, Middle East & Africa (SAMEA), Levi Strauss & Co, said in an interaction with businessline.

This comes as the company continues to see momentum in its international business. For the quarter ended May, Levi Strauss reported a net revenue of $1.6 billion, up 8 per cent year-on-year, while Asia revenue rose 10 per cent. The NYSE-listed company’s financial year starts in December.

International markets currently account for about 60 per cent of the group’s global revenue, with India among its top six markets. Its India business had reported sales of ₹1,668.7 crore in FY24, according to RoC filings, while profit declined 13.4 per cent to ₹159.4 crore.

Both its denim and non-denim businesses in India, said Gor, are growing in the mid-double digits, with women’s wear outpacing men’s. “Men’s business still makes the larger component of our business, but women’s products are growing faster,” he added.

The premium segment is also growing in high double digits, while the company’s Red Loop premium proposition accounts for about 15 per cent of its men’s business.

The shift is significant for a brand historically synonymous with jeans. Levi’s now sells more than one top for every bottom, according to Gor, with tops, non-denims, and women’s wear becoming important avenues to increase consumer engagement and wardrobe penetration.

The company is also seeing consumers buy more denim as fashion cycles create additional use cases. The shift from skinny and slim fits towards loose, baggy, wide-leg, and flare silhouettes has created more occasions to buy denim, while premium ranges such as Red Loop are targeting higher-stakes social occasions.

95% made in India

Beyond consumption, India is also becoming an important part of Levi’s supply chain. Gor said more than 95 per cent of Levi’s India consumption is made or built in India, with a broad supplier base spread across the country.

Importantly, the sourcing is not restricted to the domestic market. “India is also producing for the globe along with many other source bases across the world,” Gor said.

This could give India a larger role as global apparel supply chains diversify, particularly as the country builds integrated textile and apparel manufacturing infrastructure.

500 stores

On the retail side, Levi’s is touching its 500th store mark, a milestone Gor described as significant for the brand’s reach across consumer catchments.

Rather than setting a target for store count, Levi’s is looking to open larger stores with wider assortments in key cities and catchments, alongside its online platform, marketplaces, and shop-in-shop network.

name: H&M
title: Where did all the XXL clothes go? Fashion brands are scrapping plus sizes in the GLP-1 era
description:
The fashion juggernaut had committed to an expansion of its sizes, from XL to 4XL, and to increased body diversity of its models.
I’ve worked in the industry for over 15 years, I’ve seen the rise and fall of a lot of brands.
Drill down into the figures, though, and the reasons for the abandonment of plus-sized shoppers by mainstream fashion brands are more complex.
Even now – and despite all evidence to the contrary in visual culture – plus-sized shoppers are fashion’s vastly underserved majority.
Steiger says plus-sized shoppers speak highly of Walmart at the budget end and praises Universal Standard as a higher-end brand “founded on size inclusivity”.
text:
In March 2023, the model, activist and writer Tess Holliday announced that she had been working as a size and inclusivity consultant for H&M. The fruits of their partnership felt like “one of the most meaningful things that I’ve done in my career”, she told US Vogue at the time. The fashion juggernaut had committed to an expansion of its sizes, from XL to 4XL, and to increased body diversity of its models.

This bucked a trend, coming at an otherwise gloomy time for plus-sized fashion. By 2023, the fashion industry was in the grips of an Ozempic-fuelled celebration of skinny bodies, after its brief flirtation with curves during the body positivity movement of the late 2010s.

But by 2026, just three years after the H&M partnership was announced, the fruits of the project had vanished. Research firm Edited, which tracks items as they launch on retailers’ websites, analysed H&M’s offerings for spring/summer 2026, recording all new women’s dresses landing on the site from January to May and compared it with the same period in 2025. Last year, 3XL and 4XL made up 2% of the new inventory. This year those sizes were entirely absent. Other large sizes fell too: XXL, which had accounted for 13.3% of inventory in 2025, was down 3%, while XL was down 2%, and smaller sizes, XS to large, rose by 3% on average.

Holliday no longer works with H&M. Even when she went into the collaboration she was, “a little pessimistic”, she says. “I’ve been plus-sized my entire life. I’ve worked in the industry for over 15 years, I’ve seen the rise and fall of a lot of brands. I’m always worried whether something is genuine.” Once she began working with the brand, though, “I became very optimistic because a lot of the changes that I wanted to implement were being implemented. Unfortunately, I don’t think that maybe it was as genuine as I hoped.”

In a statement to the Guardian, H&M said that it continually monitors fit and sizing demand and confirmed that “we have chosen to discontinue sizes 3XL and 4XL, as we have seen lower demand for these sizes.”

H&M is not the only brand scaling back plus-sized garments this season. Mango, too, reduced its inventory of new dresses in sizes 16 to 20, from 6.6% in spring/summer 2025 to 0.5% in spring/summer 2026, according to Edited. Meanwhile, an analysis of dresses for sale at Anthropology during July 2026 revealed a year-on-year reduction from 10.5% to 9% in plus-sized offerings. This latest size shrinkage comes after years of other rollbacks, from closures of extended sizes ranges (Loft closed its plus-size range in 2021 after three years; Old Navy scaled back its offerings in May 2022, only nine months after launching a new plus-sized initiative). Last year, 151 locations – nearly a third of all stores – closed at the plus-sized chain Torrid. The options are so limited for plus-sized people now, says influencer Nikki Apostolou, that “I’ve given up entirely trying to go into a store or going into a mall hoping to find clothes.” Reddit is full of threads of plus-sized shoppers talking about their lack of options; some are so over it they have started sewing their own garments.

Holliday, who co-founded the #EffYourBeautyStandards campaign in 2013 seeking to foster self-love and acceptance of all body types, says she noticed the reduction first during Covid. Then, from 2022 on, she says: “There has been a rapid decline in plus-size offerings. Diversity, as a whole, is no longer a priority for a lot of brands.”

Many analysts, such as Impact Analytics’ CEO, Prashant Agrawal, pin the most recent changes in sizing to GLP-1s, which Agrawal describes as the “number one reason” apparel retailers are anxious about sizes at the moment.

Mintel’s latest research says that 18% of US adults reported using GLP-1 drugs as of June 2025, up from 12% in 2024. The impact on the average American body size has already been significant: the rate of US adult obesity appeared to peak, after rising for decades, at 39.9% in 2022, and it dropped to 36.4% this year, according to Gallup.

“It’s like nothing that anybody’s ever experienced,” says Agrawal. Before now, “each year, over the last 50 years, the US has grown bigger. This is the first time the US has gone the other way.” His company’s data, which draws from sales figures from an undisclosed number of large US apparel retailers, shows two years of rising sales of small garments (size XS up 0.45% between 2023 and 2024 and 0.43% between 2024 and 2025), and minor declines in medium (down 0.05% and 0.02%), large (down 0.31% and 0.30%) and sizes XL and larger (down 0.38% and 0.39%). In brands that order billions of units of garments in advance of each season, such small percentage points could represent a big financial, and environmental, liability.

Drill down into the figures, though, and the reasons for the abandonment of plus-sized shoppers by mainstream fashion brands are more complex. Even in the GLP-1 era, after all, the majority of Americans are still plus-sized, including those who have lost weight on GLP-1s. The latest research suggests that most GLP1 users lose between 10% and 20% of their body weight; last year Jack Plunkett, CEO of Plunkett Research, estimated that 66% of US women still wear size 14 or above, which most brands classify as plus-sized. Even now – and despite all evidence to the contrary in visual culture – plus-sized shoppers are fashion’s vastly underserved majority.

Many plus-sized customers have given up on new clothes and are turning to the secondhand market. ThredUp, like many other used clothing platforms, reports a surge in donations of larger garments in recent years (listings were up 32% year over year in the first half of 2026, and have doubled since the first half of 2023.) But they have also seen a remarkable uptick in demand. So far this year, purchase volume for large, XL and plus-sized items in women’s apparel grew 17.4% – more than double the 6.8% growth rate for small and medium.

“Demand for larger sizes isn’t fading, it’s one of the fastest-growing parts of our marketplace,” says Kristen Brophy, senior vice-president of marketing at ThredUp. The company has no data on whether this is related to GLP-1 usage, but Brophy says that resale has long played a part in shopping when people’s bodies are changing. “We’ve also heard from customers that many brick-and-mortar thrift stores don’t accept or stock plus-size items in the first place, which pushes even more of that shopping behavior online.”

Brittany Steiger, associate principal of retail and e-commerce at Mintel, says that GLP-1s are affecting the market – but that impact should be kept in perspective. “GLP-1s are changing the size curve, but they’re not eliminating the need for size inclusivity. Sixty-nine percent of shoppers say brands need to offer more size and length options. The bigger story isn’t shrinking bodies – it’s the ongoing challenge of fit.” In her view, the opportunity for brands is to concentrate on size flexibility and adjustability – and more brands are indeed incorporating elements such as hidden drawstrings, according to Edited – rather than offering fewer sizes.

Edited senior retail analyst Krista Corrigan says that the flow of traffic isn’t all going the same way. Anthropology, for example, which typically serves an affluent customer base, “is showing a pronounced ‘GLP-1 effect” not only in pruning larger garments but in switching many of its garments from numeric to alpha sizes. Corrigan says it’s because alpha sizes – size medium rather than size 14, for example – are deemed more likely to “absorb minor body fluctuations better than tailored numeric fits”, making them less prone to fit issues “for consumers undergoing body transitions”. Anthropology customers, she says, “are probably the demographic that would be adopting these GLP-1 most”.

Walmart, meanwhile, which typically serves budget-conscious shoppers, was a rare example of a brand adding inventory for larger customers this season. “That makes a lot of sense,” says Corrigan, “they’re doing something very smart and continuing to keep that thread of inclusion throughout most of their assortment, capitalizing on some of that white space.”

What this suggests, though, is that plus-sized people are being ejected from the affluent and trend-led part of the market more quickly than elsewhere. A correlation which tracks with hundreds of years of celebrity culture (Wallis Simpson, who reportedly coined the phrase “you can never be too rich or too thin”, would have loved Mounjaro) and economic reality – the inverse association between economic advantage and body mass index within western societies has been established by multiple studies. Semaglutide, which is unaffordable for many, only deepens this divide (one recent study of 4.5 million adults in Denmark showed that the proportion of individuals with a redeemed semaglutide prescription increased with income, even though the proportion living with obesity decreased.)

Despite that correlation, the US size 14-plus market is so substantial – literally tens of millions of people – that the assumption Holliday feels retailers make, all-too-readily, that all plus-sized people “can’t afford to shop anyway” is clearly untrue. For Holliday, it ties into other stereotypes she is sick of hearing. People “assume that we’re lazy or that we’re uneducated or a lot of other things”, she says. “There’s a really big disconnect, and it just boils down to the fact that plus-size people are seen as less than. Until we fix that issue in society we’re always going to keep having the same conversations over and over, because they don’t see us as worthy customers.”

Some cherished brands remain. Holliday recommends Lazy Oaf, a British brand she buys whenever she is in the UK, as well as Eloquii and Torrid, even if the latter can be frustrating on price, she says. Apostolou goes to Lane Bryant for bras and likes Target’s Wild Fable line for on-trend clothes, as well as Eloquii – though she feels they have gone downhill – for special occasion dresses. Steiger says plus-sized shoppers speak highly of Walmart at the budget end and praises Universal Standard as a higher-end brand “founded on size inclusivity”. Also at the higher end, Apostolou is into RCA Public Label, and says she wants to try to support small, plus-sized designers when she can, “designers who are working for themselves, not part of corporations who will swing wherever the wind blows them”.

For Apostolou, it is a lack of care and investment that lead so many plus-sized ranges to fail. “So many of the brands that do exist are giving us versions of things they’ve been offering since 2010. They feel like, OK, you have to hide your stomach, wear these jeans that are gonna squish you in. Wear this cold shoulder top – it’s like the plus-sized uniform – because your shoulder is the only skin that you should be allowed to show. Or it’s the same dress – here’s the cleavage and the rest is a tent.”

The narrative around Ozempic, she argues, is an excuse for fashion brands to cut back and not have to think about plus sizes. “They’ve been using every excuse that they possibly could think of for years now – ‘oh well, people aren’t shopping’ – when they’re offering the ugliest, most hideous styles ever.”

Delta & Starlink: The Story So Far According to reporting on the matter by Business Insider, Musk previously claimed that Delta would lose customers over its decision to select Amazon Leo over Starlink for its WiFi provision this year.
In truth, the discourse between Delta Air Lines and Starlink stretches back considerably further.
text:
Opinionated entrepreneur Elon Musk has taken aim at Delta Air Lines amid claims that passengers are avoiding the Atlanta-based US 'big three' legacy carrier and SkyTeam member due to its lack of Starlink WiFi. Never one to mince his words when it comes to online flame wars (such as his public spat with Ryanair Group CEO Michael O'Leary), Musk even said that things will "get much worse" for Delta.

It isn't that Delta does not offer its passengers the option to connect to onboard WiFi. While not a necessity for everyone, a total lack of connectivity would surely see any legacy carrier left in the dust by its rivals. However, Delta's decision to choose Amazon over Starlink, an arm of Musk's SpaceX firm, rubbed the businessman the wrong way, and he is now taking glee in seeing flyers vote with their feet.

Musk Claims The Situation Will "Get Much Worse"

Over time, WiFi has become a more important part of the airline passenger experience. While planes used to be a refuge from the online world and a welcome chance to disconnect for a few hours, changing passenger needs have seen WiFi become as much a part of modern flying as food and drink. Now Starlink boss Elon Musk is claiming that flyers are specifically avoiding Delta over its lack of Starlink.

Yesterday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO took to X to allege that he "warned them" about flyers voting with their feet, adding that "it will get much worse." It is worth noting that Musk's post was a quote of an image that featured just two Delta flyers claiming to have booked with United instead due to the WiFi situation. As such, it remains to be seen if there is any widespread substance to Musk's bold online claims.

Simple Flying has reached out to Delta Air Lines for comment on Musk's latest statements. We will update our coverage upon receiving a response from the carrier.

Delta & Starlink: The Story So Far

According to reporting on the matter by Business Insider, Musk previously claimed that Delta would lose customers over its decision to select Amazon Leo over Starlink for its WiFi provision this year. However, the publication noted that Delta CEO Ed Bastian backed his airline's position shortly thereafter, citing Amazon Leo's "great retailing capability and Amazon Prime and video gaming technologies."

In truth, the discourse between Delta Air Lines and Starlink stretches back considerably further. Indeed, as early as April 2022, Simple Flying reported that the carrier was testing the SpaceX-backed WiFi solution, having held preliminary talks with the company. At the time, its existing WiFi was being provided by Viasat. However, just over four years later, the news broke that it had chosen Amazon Leo instead.

A key motivation behind this choice was the ability for the carrier to prioritize its own brand and integrate the Delta Sync portal into the WiFi offering. These branding issues were ultimately what caused Delta's talks with Starlink to collapse. However, the decision has not been met with universal acclaim: Simple Flying recently reported that an ex-Delta pilot had taken to X to ask the airline to reconsider the move.

More & More Airlines Are Choosing Starlink

While Musk himself is seen by many to be a somewhat divisive character, the commercial aviation sector's response to Starlink has been more universally positive. This has been evidenced by the growing number of carriers that have equipped their aircraft with the fast and free WiFi solution in order to improve their connectivity. Qatar Airways was among the first, launching the solution back in October 2024.

Riders in the Croatian capital of Zagreb are now able to order a Pony.ai robotaxi on the Uber platform.

The move is part of an agreement between Pony.ai and Uber Technologies to deploy more than 2,000 Pony.ai robotaxis across Europe.

Pony.ai operates paid, fully-driverless services in four Chinese cities.

The plan is to add services in four other cities in Europe, with deployment in the Middle East also on the roadmap.

Uber has been active in the autonomous vehicle space, signing an agreement this year with automaker Stellantis, AI company Wayve.

It also plans with WeRide to jointly launch Spain’s first commercial robotaxi pilot.

Three core functions

Pony.ai says three core functions are required to operate robotaxi services at scale:

Level 4 (L4) autonomous driving technology

A mobility platform

Day-to-day fleet operations.

It allows technology, platform and fleet partners to work together in the same market, while individual partners may also take on more than one role.

Vehicle funding and ownership can sit with different partners, depending on the market.

For the new partnership, Pony.ai will provide its L4 autonomous driving technology, rider experience and operational expertise.

Uber will provide customer access through its global mobility platform, including booking, payment and customer service capabilities.

Day-to-day fleet operations may be carried out by established local fleet partners selected for each market.

Zagreb service

For example, the new Zagreb service is operated by local provider Verne.

Riders will be able to access robotaxis in the city – including the city centre – from 7am to 9pm, with the service set to expand over time.

At this stage, a human operator will also be on board, monitoring behind the wheel, before fully-driverless operations begin in the future, Pony.ai says.

The company was founded in China in 2016 and began collaborating with Uber in May 2025.

“This expanded agreement marks an important new phase in the partnership between Pony.ai and Uber,” said James Peng, founder and CEO of Pony.ai.

“It reflects our shared commitment to bringing safe, reliable robotaxi services to more European cities.”

Sarfraz Maredia, global head of autonomous mobility and delivery at Uber, says: “The next chapter for autonomous mobility is about moving from individual launches to repeatable commercial scale.”

“Together with Pony.ai, we’re combining advanced autonomous technology with Uber’s hybrid platform, on-the-ground experience and operational excellence to build a model that can quickly and reliably expand across cities.”

title: Walmart sees slowest pace in US comparable sales in 6 years, offers cautious guidance
description:
Comparable sales in U.S. stores, which measure sales at stores open at least a year along with online sales tied to those locations, rose 2.6% in the second quarter.
Some of the slowing growth was related to how pharmacies are regulated in the U.S., including those in Walmart stores.
Excluding the wellness category that includes Walmart’s pharmacies, comparable sales increased 3.4% in the second quarter.
For the third quarter, Walmart expects earnings per share of 62 cents to 64 cents.
The forecasts are below analysts’ expectations of 68 cents per share and sales of $188.19 billion, according to FactSet.
text:
NEW YORK -- Walmart experienced the slowest growth in comparable sales at U.S. stores in six years in its most recent quarter and it offered a cautious outlook for the year, sending shares down 6% before the opening bell Thursday.

Comparable sales in U.S. stores, which measure sales at stores open at least a year along with online sales tied to those locations, rose 2.6% in the second quarter. They rose 4.1% in the previous quarter.

Some of the slowing growth was related to how pharmacies are regulated in the U.S., including those in Walmart stores. Federal legislations require pharmacies to dispense some high-cost Medicare drugs at capped prices, the retailer said.

Excluding the wellness category that includes Walmart’s pharmacies, comparable sales increased 3.4% in the second quarter. However, even accounting for regulations, the sales were still below industry analyst expectations for a 3.8% increase, according to FactSet.

Walmart’s U.S. e-commerce business, which has become an engine of growth for the retailer, rose 24%, trailing the first-quarter pace of 26%.

Walmart is among the first batch of major retailers to report second-quarter results, which could offer industry analysts and economists another read on whether ongoing price pressures from the conflict in Iran have impacted consumer behavior.

Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base. More than 150 million customers are on its website or in its stores every week, according to Walmart.

That may draw even more attention this quarter after U.S. data released Friday showed that retail sales were surprisingly weak in July and a new read on consumers from the University of Michigan revealed growing pessimism about the economy, with so many Americans struggling with higher costs for gas, groceries and just about everything else.

The new figures from Walmart revealed the smallest gain in comparable store sales since a 1.9% gain for the quarter ended Jan. 31, 2020, according to FactSet.

That has broadened Walmart’s customer base and the retailer has begun capturing a larger share of wealthier Americans. The biggest gains in market share for Walmart are coming from households with annual incomes over $100,000.

Walmart’s quarterly net income was $6.37 billion, or 80 cents per share, in the three-month period ended July 31. Adjusted per-share results were 81 cents, easily topping the 74 cents Wall Street had expected, according to FactSet.

Sales rose 5.9% to $187.94 billion. Analysts were predicting $186.62 billion, according to FactSet.

For the third quarter, Walmart expects earnings per share of 62 cents to 64 cents. It projects sales to be up 3% to 3.5%. That would put sales in a range of $184.88 billion to $186.23 billion. The forecasts are below analysts’ expectations of 68 cents per share and sales of $188.19 billion, according to FactSet.

For the full year, Walmart now expects earnings per share to be in the range of $2.80 to $2.87 while sales should be up anywhere from 4% to 5%. That would mean a forecast for sales in the range of $741.7 billion to $748.8 billion, according to FactSet.

Analysts expected $2.90 per share and sales of $752.06 billion for the year, according to FactSet.

text:
Riders in Zagreb become the first in Europe to book an AV through Uber, powered by Pony.ai and operated by Verne.

ZAGREB, Croatia, August 19, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Uber Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: UBER), Verne and Pony AI Inc. ("Pony.ai") (NASDAQ: PONY; HKEX: 2026) today announced the launch of autonomous rides on the Uber app in Zagreb, marking the first time riders in Europe can book an AV with Uber.

From today, riders can book an autonomous ride within key areas of Zagreb, including the city centre, with service availability and geographic coverage set to expand over time. At launch, a licensed operator will be on-board monitoring behind the wheel, as part of our phased introduction, before fully driverless operations begin in the future.

The new service brings together Pony.ai's autonomous driving technology, Verne's service ecosystem and operational framework, and Uber's global mobility platform. Under this model, Pony.ai provides its autonomous driving solution; Verne acts as fleet owner and service operator; and Uber integrates the service into its ride-hailing network and delivers the rider experience via its app.

The launch builds on the partnership announced in March, moving the service from development and testing to real-world deployment on Uber.

"Today marks a major milestone for autonomous mobility in Europe," said Annie Duvnjak, Global Head of Autonomous Mobility Operations at Uber. "By bringing together Pony.ai's proven autonomous-driving technology, Verne's operational expertise and Uber's global platform, we're making it simple for riders to access autonomous rides through the Uber app. Zagreb is an important first step as we work to bring AVs to millions of riders and build the world's largest platform for AV deployment."

Zagreb is the first market to launch under the partnership and provides a model that the companies plan to scale to additional European cities. Further details on the next markets to launch will be announced later this year.

"Verne launched Europe's first commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb in April. Since then, we have completed thousands of autonomous rides, operating every day and learning from real customers in a real European city. From today, Verne rides are also available through Uber, giving customers another way to access the service. This marks another European first — the first time autonomous rides are available through Uber in Europe," said Marko Pejkovic, CEO of Verne, "This is an important milestone not only for Verne, but also for Croatia. A service pioneered here in Zagreb is now available through the world's largest mobility platform. The experience we are gaining every day in Zagreb will help us bring Verne to other European cities."

title: Aussie beauty brand Sasy n Savy expands into South Korean retail
description:
But as Korean skincare continues to capture Australian consumers and retail shelf space, one homegrown beauty brand is reversing the flow, expanding into South Korea itself.
Australian beauty heads to Korea Australian skincare and wellness brand Sasy n Savy has expanded its South Korean retail presence, launching into Galleria Department Store Gwanggyo and AK Department Store Bundang earlier this month.
That makes Sasy n Savy’s expansion notable beyond the addition of two new retail doors.
The company says South Korea forms part of a broader international growth strategy rather than representing a standalone retail expansion.
“Our goal is to build Sasy n Savy into an internationally recognised Australian skincare brand,” Maakrun said.
text:
K-beauty is booming in Australia. But as Korean skincare continues to capture Australian consumers and retail shelf space, one homegrown beauty brand is reversing the flow, expanding into South Korea itself.

Australia’s appetite for Korean beauty shows little sign of slowing. Once a relatively niche corner of the beauty market, K-beauty has moved firmly into the Australian mainstream, spanning specialist retailers, pharmacies, department stores and major beauty destinations.

The numbers tell the story. As previously reported by Retail Beauty, according to Future Market Insights, Australians are now the biggest global spenders per capita on South Korean beauty products outside Korea itself, fuelled by social media, K-pop celebrity influence and the reputation of K-beauty formulations for innovation and efficacy.

And the growth has been rapid. In 2024, South Korea accounted for 10.8 per cent of Australian imports across the HS 3304 cosmetics category, with imports from Korea increasing 32.8 per cent year-on-year.

But while Korean brands are increasingly looking to Australia for growth, one Australian skincare company is making the journey in reverse.

Australian beauty heads to Korea

Australian skincare and wellness brand Sasy n Savy has expanded its South Korean retail presence, launching into Galleria Department Store Gwanggyo and AK Department Store Bundang earlier this month.

Founded in Australia in 2000 by Samea Maakrun, Sasy n Savy offers skincare, body care, hair care, sun protection and wellness products, with its formulations combining Australian botanical ingredients with a vegan and organic-led brand positioning.

For an Australian brand, entering South Korea represents an interesting proposition. Korea isn’t simply another international beauty market; it is one of the industry’s most influential centres for formulation, product innovation, manufacturing and emerging skincare trends.

“Korea is recognised globally for its sophisticated beauty consumers and strong appreciation for quality skincare. To have Sasy n Savy available through leading department stores such as Galleria and AK is an important step in our international growth,” Maakrun said.

Reversing the K-Beauty flow

The significance of the expansion becomes clearer when viewed against the considerable imbalance in beauty trade between the two countries.

In 2025, Australian imports of South Korean beauty and skincare preparations reached US$180.07 million in 2025, according to UN Comtrade data. Australian exports in the same category heading to South Korea totalled just US$8.71 million. That makes Sasy n Savy’s expansion notable beyond the addition of two new retail doors.

While Australian consumers increasingly look to Korea for beauty innovation, the brand is betting there is also an opportunity for Australian beauty propositions — particularly those built around Australian botanicals and wellness — within the highly competitive Korean market.

The company says South Korea forms part of a broader international growth strategy rather than representing a standalone retail expansion.

“Our goal is to build Sasy n Savy into an internationally recognised Australian skincare brand,” Maakrun said. “Entering the Korean market allows us to introduce our products to a new audience while continuing to grow our brand internationally.”

From K-Beauty to A-Beauty?

The expansion also raises a broader question for Australia’s beauty industry. Korean brands have demonstrated how a distinct national beauty identity can become an international commercial proposition. Australia’s own combination of botanical ingredients, wellness heritage, natural beauty positioning and established skincare expertise offers local brands a potentially differentiated story abroad.

For Sasy n Savy, entering one of the world’s most sophisticated and competitive skincare markets will put that proposition to the test.

At a time when Australia can’t seem to get enough of K-beauty, this Australian brand is betting Korean consumers might be ready for a little more A-beauty in return.

title: Qcells and Microsoft expand AI energy alliance - Hanwha Group
description:
Today, Qcells announced they are expanding their existing relationship with Microsoft to explore ways to pair AI infrastructure with new energy capacity.
The collaboration supports Microsoft’s Community-First AI Infrastructure initiative and Qcells’ growing role in developing the energy infrastructure that enables AI.
Qcells would bring its expertise across energy development, engineering, procurement, construction, and grid orchestration to help turn Microsoft’s interest into new energy infrastructure.
This new collaboration represents the next phase of that relationship as the companies explore new approaches to supporting America’s growing AI infrastructure.
About Qcells Qcells is a leading clean energy company delivering end-to-end solutions—from advanced solar cell and panel manufacturing to intelligent energy storage systems and large-scale EPC services.
text:
Artificial intelligence is creating a new challenge for the electric grid: how to add computing capacity without shifting costs onto the communities that host it. Today, Qcells announced they are expanding their existing relationship with Microsoft to explore ways to pair AI infrastructure with new energy capacity. Rather than simply adding electricity demand to the grid, the proposed approach would develop new generation and flexible energy resources alongside Microsoft’s expanding data center footprint, helping support grid reliability while enabling future AI growth. The collaboration supports Microsoft’s Community-First AI Infrastructure initiative and Qcells’ growing role in developing the energy infrastructure that enables AI.

Under a proposed “bring-your-own-capacity” (BYOC) model, Qcells would develop and build new energy capacity that could be delivered either directly to Microsoft or to the local utility serving the surrounding community. Microsoft would fund the power required for its operations, helping ensure that new data center demand is matched with new energy resources. Qcells would bring its expertise across energy development, engineering, procurement, construction, and grid orchestration to help turn Microsoft’s interest into new energy infrastructure.

The companies are also exploring Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) that combine thousands of residential and commercial batteries into a single flexible energy resource. During periods of peak demand, those batteries can provide electricity to the grid when utilities need it most. Outside of those events, participating customers would use their batteries normally while benefiting from lower electricity bills and compensation for supporting grid operations.

Qcells plans to prioritize participation from income-qualified households, helping to ensure that the economic benefits of AI infrastructure extend into the communities where it is built. Microsoft Fabric and Azure are the unifying data layers that enable secure coordination of these distributed energy resources (DERs) at scale.

“As AI transforms the economy, we have an opportunity to rethink how the energy infrastructure supporting it is built,” said Andy Park, Global CEO of Qcells. “Our relationship with Microsoft began with American-made solar manufacturing and construction. Now we’re exploring how we can build the energy capacity needed for AI while creating lasting value for the communities that share the grid.”

Qcells began working with Microsoft in 2023 through an agreement for 2.5 gigawatts (GW) of American-made solar modules and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) services. In 2024, the companies expanded that alliance to 12 GW, creating the largest solar supply and EPC agreement of its kind. This new collaboration represents the next phase of that relationship as the companies explore new approaches to supporting America’s growing AI infrastructure.

About Qcells

Qcells is a leading clean energy company delivering end-to-end solutions—from advanced solar cell and panel manufacturing to intelligent energy storage systems and large-scale EPC services.
